title: Camp life: tents, cold, cabbage soup and civilian status
summary: Internees were treated as civilians, organised like a small city, and endured cold and worm-filled soup until the committee improved conditions during almost three years.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Were these people all made to work, or -- was it a work camp was it?
No, no. It was not the same. We were internees.
Like prisoners of war.
Yes, war prisoners, yes.
And were there Americans and --

Yes, all together. All the Allies. Yes, all grouped together. And we're not considered as war prisoners, 'cause they couldn't force -- we would work if it was in the interest of our camp, to do things for our camp, we would work, but no one forced us to work, you see.
Briggs 352
I see. So if it was a question of building latrines or something like that --

Yeh, we'd do it ourselves, if it was necessary. But no one -- the Germans couldn't tell us, do so and so and so and so. Everything was organized like a little city, you see. A country within a country.
Well, what was it, all barracks or tents, or --
Yes, they were tents, more or less. Tents or small barracks were built quickly, you know.
Right. And how was it heated? It must have been pretty cold.
Yes, pretty cold. We had -- we were heated by coal stoves. We had one or two big stoves in a room. It depended on the size of the room, you see.
Briggs

And we had enough coal and everything, as far as that's concerned. And what we didn't care so much about at first, you see, we give them the cabbage soup. Cabbage soup with worms floating around on it. (Laughter).
So, you'd just scoop the worms out?

Yes, if you had nothing else to eat, you had to just scoop the worms out, and eat it. But that didn't last too long, 'cause the members of our committee forced the Germans, and as I told you, the Commander of the camp, was one of the 1418 Men of Surgage, an aristocrat. And he realized that civilians must be treated as civilians, 'cause we were civilians and not soldiers, you see.
Yes.
And that was when we did assume responsibility. We had days
Briggs 354

where we had potatoes, white potatoes, and we had what you call 'horses' heads' and everything, you know. (Laughter). You didn't eat it, but -- the potatoes were okay, and they had some white potatoes and butter, or margarina, -- it tasted pretty good. (Laughter).
Well, how long were you there?
Three years. Almost three years.
